123.0.0.en: Unto You I lift up my eyes, O You who dwell in the heavens.

123.0.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm lifts his eyes, while on the earth, to God who dwells in the heavens, and by this he declares his humility and his need of God, the High and Exalted. He entreats God and seeks His mercies.

123.0.2.en: 2- Lifting the eyes to God confirms the psalmist's faith in God and his confidence that He is able to help him and rescue him from all his troubles.

123.1.0.en: Behold, as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress, so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until He have mercy upon us.

123.1.1.en: 1- The psalm declares that we lift our eyes toward God like servants and maidens, who belong to their master and lift their eyes to him to ask of him whatever they request; perhaps he will have pity on them and give to them, or perhaps he will see fit not to give to them, and they accept; for their master sees what is suitable. And although men may err, the Lord is good, and He knows what is good for us, and gives us all that is suitable for us.

123.1.2.en: 2- Lifting the eyes toward God that He may have mercy on us shows our trust in Him and our love for Him, and our faith in His mercy and tenderness. We keep our eyes lifted until He has mercy on us, and even after this we keep looking to Him all our life, because He is a tender God, ever merciful.

123.1.3.en: Trust in God's tenderness, and ask of Him what you need, and may you remain persevering until He gives to you and fills you with peace.

123.1.4.en: Never leave Him, for we have no one but Him.

123.2.0.en: Have mercy upon us, O Lord, have mercy upon us, for we are exceedingly filled with contempt. Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorn of those that are at ease, and with the contempt of the proud.

123.2.1.en: 1- He asks for mercy and repeats it, confirming his great need and also the abundance of mockery and contempt from his enemies, and he expresses this by saying “we are filled” and “filled.” The writer of the psalm suffers great bitterness in his soul and a hard affliction, so he entreats the merciful God to lift it from him.

123.2.2.en: 2- These verses are a prophecy about Christ, who bore all our sins on the Cross, and who asks the Father to take away from Him the cup of suffering, and declares that He has been filled with contempt and mockery for the sake of our redemption.

123.2.3.en: 3- These verses express the feelings of the penitent whom the devil has wearied by mocking him.

123.2.4.en: Turn your suffering and your pains in affliction, or in falling into sin, into prayers and supplications to God your Father, who loves you and longs to have mercy on you and take away your pains; indeed, He has already lifted them on the Cross, and He desires to support you in all your troubles.

123.2.5.en: God the Savior. A song of ascents. Of David. “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, let Israel now say” (v. 1). Introduction:

123.2.6.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, as the title of the psalm states.

123.2.7.en: 2- When was it written? Late in David's life, after God had delivered him from the hands of his enemies and he had triumphed over them all.

123.2.8.en: 3- Perhaps this psalm is a prophecy about those returning from captivity after God had delivered them from the hands of the cruel Chaldeans, and they returned to Jerusalem at the beginning of the kingdom of the Medes and Persians.

123.2.9.en: 4- Perhaps this psalm is also a prophecy about Nehemiah and the Jews of his time, whom God delivered from the hand of their neighbors who opposed them: Tobiah and those with him.

123.2.10.en: 5- This psalm shows the feelings of the penitent believer who has triumphed over Satan, who thanks God and glorifies Him because He delivered him from the hand of his enemies, the demons.

123.2.11.en: 6- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms because it prophesies about Christ, especially in (v. 7).

123.2.12.en: 7- This psalm is prayed on the fifth of the steps of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

123.2.13.en: 8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, where we thank God for His love and care, by which He rescued us from the devil's wars all day long and brought us to its end.

124.0.0.en: “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side,” let Israel now say, “if it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us,

124.0.1.en: 1- David shows his faith in God and his boldness before Him when he says “the LORD who was on our side,” for He is the only protection from the enemies surrounding us. He speaks in the plural, because the wars of the demons are against all who believe in God; indeed, he calls his people Israel to declare this faith, that the God who is ours is our protection from the enemies.

124.0.2.en: 2- These are the feelings of the penitents who return to God, whom He delivered from the snares of the devil, and who rose from their falls. They are also the feelings of the captives who returned to Jerusalem and built the temple despite the opposition of the enemies around them, because the Lord was with them.

124.0.3.en: 3- These two verses are the feelings of Jacob, the patriarch, which he declared to his uncle Laban when he left him and Laban tried to bring him back by force, but God appeared to Laban and rebuked him, so he did not lay a hand on Jacob (Gen 31:42).

124.1.0.en: Then they had swallowed us up quick, when their wrath was kindled against us. Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul. Then the proud waters had gone over our soul.

124.1.1.en: Overwhelmed us: the waters carried us and flung us far away.

124.1.2.en: Proud (swelling): overflowing, that is, covering us completely.

124.1.3.en: 1- David likens the enemies to waters rushing violently like a torrent, which carry us and fling us far away, and we die from the violence of the waters. He also likens the enemies to many waters, able to flood us so that we die, as the great army of Pharaoh was able to kill all the children of Israel or return them to slavery, and as the waters of the Red Sea were able to drown the people of God. But God rescued His people and drowned the enemies.

124.1.4.en: 2- These two verses signify what happened with Christ, against whom the Jews rose up and crucified Him, and He died on the Cross; but by His death He triumphed over death, and went down to Hades, and brought Adam and his children up to Paradise. So the waters flooded Him and the torrent covered Him, but He was drowned, that is, He died on the Cross, and then rose triumphant and also rescued the humanity that believes in Him.

124.1.5.en: If you hear threats, or fears from the wicked, do not be alarmed, for they have no power before God who protects you. Hold fast to God by repeating your psalms and your prayers, and you will enjoy His fellowship within His strong fortress.

124.2.0.en: Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as a prey to their teeth.

124.2.1.en: He likens the enemies to ravenous beasts with sharp teeth and fangs, but they could not come near us and devour us because of God's protection of us; therefore David calls all believers to bless God, praise Him and glorify Him for His protection and care for them.

124.3.0.en: Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we are escaped.

124.3.1.en: 1- Here he likens Satan to the fowler, meaning by the fowler cunning and deceit. Satan sometimes fights with violence and fears, as he likened them to sweeping waters or ravenous beasts. But here Satan appears setting a snare for the man who believes in God, whom he likens to a small, weak bird, and he throws into the trap the grains that lure it. If a person rejects the lusts of the world he will not fall into the snare; and if he falls through ignorance and seeks God with faith, He breaks the snare for him, and the bird escapes and flies and gets far from the fowler. God's grace breaks the snare, while the striving lies in seeking God, and then escaping and flying far away from the snare.

124.3.2.en: 2- The bird signifies Christ, who fell into the hand of the devil on the Cross and died, but by His death He trampled death and seized Satan, that is, He broke the snare, in order to give power to His believing children, that they may escape the snares of Satan.

124.4.0.en: Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.

124.4.1.en: In this last verse David summarizes the psalm: God is the Savior, the Deliverer and the Help in every step of our life, and therefore we ought to rely on Him in everything, because He is our help and is able to help us, since He is the Creator of all things: heaven and what is in it, and earth and what is in it.

124.4.2.en: May you thank God every day for His works and His help and His care for you, so that your heart may rejoice and your faith be established, and you rejoice the heart of God, and He gives you spiritual and material gifts without measure.

124.4.3.en: The blessings of the righteous. A song of ascents. “They that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion”... v. 1. Introduction:

124.4.4.en: 1- Its writer: unknown. This psalm is considered one of the orphan psalms because the name of its writer is not mentioned in the title.

124.4.5.en: 2- This psalm speaks of God's care for His children in the Church, that is, His care for those who believe in Him and their great eternal future, and on the other hand the punishment of the wicked. It is a psalm that helps the one praying to stand firm in faith, and it carries the meaning of thanksgiving to God.

124.4.6.en: 3- This psalm is prayed on the sixth step in the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

124.4.7.en: 4- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Agpeya, in the prayer of Vespers, to help the one praying to stand firm in faith until the end of the day, indeed throughout life, and to warn him against negligence, lest the punishment of the wicked come upon him.

125.0.0.en: They that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed, but abides for ever.

125.0.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm likens those who trust in the Lord to mount Zion, which rises toward heaven higher than its surroundings, and so it signifies inclination toward spiritual and heavenly things.

125.0.2.en: 2- It is also great and firm, signifying strength and continuance.

125.0.3.en: 3- It is also lasting, that is, it remains for ever, because those who trust in God have a portion in the eternal Kingdom.

125.1.0.en: As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about His people from henceforth even for ever.

125.1.1.en: The city of Jerusalem is surrounded by mountains on its four sides; so also God surrounds it with His care. These mountains signify the holy angels who love God and His children, whom God sends to serve His children, and who always intercede for them. So Jerusalem, that is, all the believers in it, are in the care and providence of God and in the company of the saints, now in their life on the earth, and then the enjoyment of the vision of God and His care, and the communion of the saints, will be complete in the age to come.

125.2.0.en: For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity.

125.2.1.en: 1- Although the believers are in God's care, He permits trials for them, to which he refers here as the rod of the wicked; so He permits the enemies of His people to trouble them for a time, but not for ever. For if the trials increase, they may lead the righteous to despair, and if the trials lessen, they may lead to negligence and falling into iniquity. For this the Scripture says that “God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it”

125.2.2.en: (1 Cor 10:13). And God disciplines His children in a spirit of fatherhood to lead them to the straight way, as He disciplined Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, with leprosy, as a father, that she might repent and not judge Moses or murmur against him, declaring His fatherhood toward her by saying “If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days?” (Num 12:14).

125.2.3.en: Trusting in God gives you rest and peace, and establishes you in faith, and even gives you an opportunity for spiritual growth. So firmly drive away all the anxious thoughts that Satan stirs up against you, for they are foreign to you, so that you may enjoy the embrace of God.

125.3.s.en: (2) The recompense of the righteous and of the wicked

125.3.0.en: Do good, O LORD, unto those that be good, and to them that are upright in their hearts. As for such as turn aside unto their crooked ways, the LORD shall lead them forth with the workers of iniquity. But peace shall be upon Israel.

125.3.1.en: Such as turn aside unto crooked ways: those who are changed and deviate into crooked ways.

125.3.2.en: 1- The psalm ends by declaring the recompense of the righteous, which is divine goodness on the earth and in heaven, and in general they enjoy God's peace continually, because they believed and trusted in Him and lived with Him.

125.3.3.en: 2- On the other hand, the wicked who deviate from God's way and walk in the crooked ways of evil receive the punishment of their deviation and crookedness and distance from God, that is, they receive the natural result of the evil in which they lived, which is of course eternal torment; and they do not enjoy peace within them, but on the contrary are in constant turmoil and disquiet.

125.3.4.en: Look at the grace of the peace that is within you, and also at the greatness of the eternal good things, so that you may bear the toils of spiritual striving and reject the temporary pleasure of sin, and so walk in the straight way that leads to the Kingdom.

125.3.5.en: The joy of the strugglers. A song of ascents. “When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion”... v. 1. Introduction:

125.3.6.en: 1- Its writer: unknown; it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is not known.

125.3.7.en: 2- The time of its writing: at the return from captivity, whether a short time after the captivity in the days of Zerubbabel, or a long time after it in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah.

125.3.8.en: 3- This psalm is considered a song of the captives returning from captivity with joy to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, to return to their worship and to offer sacrifices to God.

125.3.9.en: 4- This psalm suits every penitent and every striver on the path of the spiritual life, who remembers God's comforts and thanks Him, and so is strengthened to complete his striving.

125.3.10.en: 5- This psalm resembles Psalm 85 and the thirty-first chapter of the Book of Jeremiah.

125.3.11.en: 6- This psalm is prayed on the seventh step on the way of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

125.3.12.en: 7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, so that the spiritual striver may remember God's work with him throughout the day, to be comforted and to complete his striving and his spiritual vigilance for the rest of the day and during the night.

126.0.0.en: When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream.

126.0.1.en: 1- When the children of Israel returned from captivity to Jerusalem, they were in joy and incredulous wonder, so that they thought they were in a dream during the night. This is an expression of the intensity of their joy, because God's work was beyond imagination, not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles who heard of their return.

126.0.2.en: 2- Likewise the penitent who returns to God, after He removes his sin and he returns to his purity and lives in fellowship with God, is in inexpressible joy.

126.1.0.en: Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing. Then said they among the Gentiles, “The LORD has done great things for them.” The LORD has done great things for us, whereof we are glad.

126.1.1.en: The children of Israel rejoiced at the decree of Cyrus, the Persian king, that they should return to Jerusalem to build the temple.

126.1.2.en: They began to regain their longing for worship in the house of the Lord, and even began to sing the spiritual songs that their fathers had been accustomed to say before the house of the Lord. They were in great joy, which the nations around them witnessed, and they marveled at God's wonderful work, and the joy of the children of Israel became a preaching without words to the nations, that they might believe in the mighty God, who is above all gods.

126.1.3.en: Ask the Lord to help you in your striving to be rid of your sins, so that you praise Him and glorify Him and live in joy amid the pains of this life, and so become a light to the world, which suffers many afflictions.

126.2.0.en: Turn again our captivity, O LORD, as the streams in the south.

126.2.1.en: 1- About 50,000 persons of the captives returned with Zerubbabel in the first return, then about 4,000 in the second return with Ezra, while the third return, with Nehemiah, was a very limited number. The rest of the Jews in captivity were occupied with trade and their business and projects, so their hearts were not moved to worship God in His temple. Therefore the writer of the psalm prays to God to bring back the rest of the captives, whose hearts had dried up from the love of God, like the streams found south of Jerusalem, at the end of watercourses that are dry throughout the summer; but in the winter season the warm winds coming from the south move the clouds, and the rains fall and fill the water channels, and the streams flow.

126.2.2.en: 2- The captives occupied with trade and business in Babylon signify the believers in every generation who are occupied with the lusts of the world, whose hearts have dried up like dry watercourses; so we ask that God move their hearts to return to Him, like the streams of the south.

126.3.0.en: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goes forth and weeps, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

126.3.1.en: 1- The farmer toils in preparing the ground, sowing the seeds and caring for his crop until it grows, bearing many toils, so that his tears flow from the great effort he makes, but in the end he rejoices when he reaps this crop and gathers it in sheaves.

126.3.2.en: 2- This sower signifies the spiritual striver who toils in his striving against sin and his pursuit of acquiring the virtues, and perseveres many days, but in the end he will surely rejoice when he receives God's spiritual blessings in his life, and so enjoys purity and peace and the spiritual virtues, and above all fellowship with God, which is the pledge of the everlasting heavenly joy. Whoever toils in his spiritual striving on the earth will surely receive God's grace in the joys of the Kingdom.

126.3.3.en: God has prepared for you a great crown in the heavens, so may you look to it at the beginning of every day, that you may fight the good fight; and if you fall, rise quickly and continue your striving, and be confident that God's grace will help you to receive your crown.

126.3.4.en: The blessings of God. A song of ascents. Of Solomon. “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it.) “.. v. 1) Introduction:

126.3.5.en: 1- Its writer: Solomon, as stated in the title of the psalm, and there are two opinions about Solomon as its writer: a- Solomon the well-known king who built the temple.

126.3.6.en: b- Solomon is a title of Zerubbabel, who returned with the first company of the captives, and he was called Solomon because he was of the seed of Solomon, since Zerubbabel was of the royal line. This is the more probable opinion, because in the days of Zerubbabel there was opposition to the building of the temple, but God made the Jews prosper, and they built the temple and Jerusalem and its walls.

126.3.7.en: 2- When was it written? After the return from captivity.

126.3.8.en: 3- This psalm suits every believer who prays and suffers afflictions, and so trusts in God's power and relies on Him.

126.3.9.en: 4- This psalm speaks of the two prophets, and the next psalm speaks of the wife and the prophetess; therefore these two psalms are considered psalms of the family and of God's work in it.

126.3.10.en: 5- This psalm used to be chanted for the woman after her childbirth, as thanksgiving to God and a blessing for the mother who had given birth.

126.3.11.en: 6- This psalm is prayed on the eighth step on the way of the ascent to the temple of the Lord.

126.3.12.en: 7- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, to confirm an important truth, namely that the Lord is the foundation of life and the supporter of the believer in all his steps; so it lifts the heart in thanksgiving to God and establishes it in relying on God.
